title: Two Giant Planets Are Fluffier Than Cotton Candy!
summary:
Imagine a planet as big as Jupiter but lighter than cotton candy. That's what astronomers just found! Two giant exoplanets, named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, are so puffy they belong to a rare club called "super-puffs." They orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth. That's super far away!

The first clue came from volunteers looking at data from NASA's TESS space telescope. They noticed tiny dips in the star's brightness. Those dips meant planets were passing in front of the star. To confirm, scientists used telescopes around the world. The ASTEP observatory in Antarctica was perfect because the winter darkness there lasts all day. They recorded transits (when a planet crosses in front of its star) that lasted more than 11 hours. Those were the longest complete planetary transits ever seen from the ground!

The two planets dance around their star in a pattern. For every five orbits the inner planet makes, the outer one makes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust.

Scientists still don't know how super-puffs form. One idea is that they have big fluffy atmospheres of hydrogen and helium around small rocky cores. That would make them look huge but stay very light. Next, the team will use the James Webb Space Telescope to study their air. Maybe we'll finally learn how these cotton-candy planets are made!
why_it_matters: Learning how faraway planets form helps us understand our own solar system — and it shows that kid volunteers can help make real space discoveries.

background_read: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system — more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. The new planets are about that big, but far lighter.
NASA's TESS space telescope (a satellite that watches faraway stars for tiny changes in their light) has been hunting for planets since 2018, and volunteers help check the data it sends back.
The James Webb Space Telescope (the most powerful space telescope ever built, launched in 2021) can study the air around faraway planets better than any telescope before it.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers, plus volunteers who studied data from NASA's TESS space telescope and scientists who used telescopes around the world.
WHAT: They found two giant 'super-puff' exoplanets, TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, that are huge but extremely light.
WHERE: The planets orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth, and extra checks came from the ASTEP observatory in Antarctica.
WHY: Scientists want to learn how super-puffs form and will use the James Webb Space Telescope to study their air.

perspectives.description: These planets are so light and puffy that they could teach us brand-new things about how planets are born.
Nobody knows yet how super-puffs form, so the team needs more telescope time before they can be sure of anything.
Volunteers who spotted the tiny dips in the star's light show that anyone, even kids, can help find real planets.
